_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-06) review fixes: the sim's single-database layout now matches the story (power cut at 04:12, power back at 05:37, app servers up at 05:41, the database rebuilt from the 02:00 snapshot until 07:05, 11 bookings lost; with a standby in AZ-c the site keeps serving and loses 0), with a new bookings-lost stat and bookings arriving one every 12 minutes as on Tuesday night; sim.lede and sim.tryThis describe that run; the story says the rebuild took until 7:05; reply option C now loses one booking and stays dark almost three hours, matching the sim's booking rate and outage; the senior answer's Part 2 says the app servers in AZ-b and AZ-c carried the load, matching the cold case's three app servers; realWorld[0] now uses AWS's own times (power lost at 4:11 AM PST, restored at 4:55 AM) instead of The Register's 5:39 AM, The Register's facts get their own entry, and the AWS status text is cited from Pagely's status page instead of InfluxData's.
title: Lost in the Cloud
setting: a ferry company moving its servers

post.author: u/harbor_ops_maren
post.title: We moved our ferry bookings into the cloud so the harbor couldn't flood them again. Last Tuesday at 4:12 AM, the cloud went dark. Only our part of it.

blocks.text: I run operations for Greywater Ferries: three boats, four islands, the first sailing at 5:40 AM. Our booking system used to live on a server in the harbor office, until the harbor came into the harbor office. Twice. So last spring we moved to the cloud, which our IT man, Sol, describes as someone else's data centers, rented by the hour.

He explained the map. The cloud company splits the world into regions, each a cluster of data centers in one area. Each region is split into availability zones, AZs: one or more data centers each, miles from the other zones, with their own power and cooling. Our servers are virtual machines, software computers carved out of the company's real ones. Sol made two of them to run the booking app, plus a database server, and put all three in AZ-b, close together, so they'd talk fast.

Last Tuesday at 4:12 AM the booking site went dark, and so did the ticket scanners on the dock. The cloud company's status page said a single data center in a single availability zone had lost power, in AZ-b. Ours. The dashboard still listed our three machines. Their health checks said nothing answered.

04:12  booking-app-1  (AZ-b)  health check failed
04:12  booking-app-2  (AZ-b)  health check failed
04:12  bookings-db    (AZ-b)  no connection
05:37  power restored in AZ-b
05:41  booking-app-1, booking-app-2  ok
07:05  bookings-db restored from 02:00 snapshot

Power came back at 5:37. Our app servers woke up. The database's disk had been damaged, and Sol rebuilt it from last night's snapshot, a copy of its disk saved at 2:00 AM. That took until 7:05. We sailed the 5:40 and the 6:30 with a handwritten list. Eleven bookings made between 2:00 and 4:12 were simply gone. Eleven people came down the dock that morning holding tickets our system says were never sold.
Somewhere there's a building none of us has ever seen, and our tickets went dark inside it.

The fishing co-op on the next pier uses the same cloud company. Their auction app didn't blink. Their manager says it lives "in all three zones". Sol says ours could too, but it would cost more and he isn't sure how. Our owner asks a simpler question: why did we pay to move into the cloud if the cloud can go dark? What do I tell her?

blocks.label: where_our_servers_live.png

diagram.aria: Greywater's corner of the cloud. Passengers and dock scanners reach the booking app. In the North Coast region there are three availability zones. AZ-a and AZ-c hold nothing of Greywater's. AZ-b, which lost power at 4:12 AM, holds both booking app servers and the bookings database, whose disk was damaged and which came back at 7:05 AM.

blocks.caption: Sol drew our corner of the cloud on the back of a timetable. One region, three zones, and everything we own in the one that lost power. The other two zones had power all morning. We had nothing there.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: The cloud didn't go dark. One data center did, in one zone, and you'd put every egg you own in it. Zones exist so you don't have to. Spread your two app servers across two zones behind your load balancer, so either one can carry the day alone. Then ask your cloud company what a standby database in another zone would cost, and compare it with Tuesday.

replies.author: u/harbor_ops_maren
replies.text: Sol says the cloud company's managed database can do that with one setting. Ours isn't managed. He installed it himself on a virtual machine.

comments.author: u/tide_table_tomas
comments.text: A managed service is one where the cloud company runs the software for you, here the database: backups, updates, and, if you tick the box, a standby. That's a second copy in another zone that gets every write as it happens, and if the first copy dies, the service switches to the standby by itself. That switch is called failover. You pay for both copies, of course.

comments.author: u/co_op_auctioneer
comments.text: That's us next door. Three app servers, one per zone, and a database with a standby in a second zone. Tuesday at 4:12 we got an alert that the database had failed over. A minute or two of errors while it switched. That was our whole morning.

comments.author: u/fogbound_fern
comments.text: "Someone else's data centers" is the most honest description of the cloud I've heard. Someone else's, and somewhere else.

reply.prompt: Sol can rebuild before the winter timetable starts. What should he build? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Spread the app servers across at least two zones behind the load balancer, and move the database to a managed service with a standby in another zone. Keep the nightly snapshots too.
options.part2: Sol spent two weekends on it. In February the cloud company had another power problem, in AZ-a this time, where one app server and our main database now live. The app servers in AZ-b and AZ-c took every request. The database failed over to its standby in AZ-c by itself, and the booking site showed errors for about a minute and a half. Then it carried on. Nobody on the dock noticed. The scanners logged one strange thing that morning: a ticket scanned at 4:13 for the 5:40, for a seat we stopped selling when the old harbor office flooded.
options.senior: Spread every layer across zones: app servers behind a load balancer, and a database with a standby in another zone that takes over by itself. Any one zone can fail, so design for losing any one. Keep backups as well, because a standby copies mistakes as faithfully as it copies data.

options.text: Move everything back to a server in the harbor office, where we can see it.
options.part2: We bought a new server and put it on a shelf, a meter above the last flood line. In March a storm took out the harbor's power for six hours. The server sat in the dark with everything we own on it, exactly like Tuesday, except this time it was our building.
options.senior: A server you can see is still one building, one power supply and one flood. Zones give you separate buildings you could never afford yourself, but only if you use more than one.

options.text: Keep everything in AZ-b, but take a database snapshot every 15 minutes instead of every night.
options.verdict: Trade-off. Loses less, still goes dark
options.part2: At the next outage, Sol rebuilt the database from a snapshot taken eight minutes before the power went. We lost one booking instead of eleven. The site was still dark for almost three hours, and the 5:40 still sailed with a handwritten list.
options.senior: More frequent snapshots shrink how much you lose, not how long you're down: everything still sits in one zone. Backups and a standby solve different problems, and you usually want both.

options.text: Move to a different cloud company whose data centers don't lose power.
options.part2: Sol spent a month moving us. The new company's status page has a green tick next to every zone. In April, one of their zones lost cooling for most of a night. We were in it, all of us, in the one zone.
options.senior: Any data center can lose power or cooling. That's the reason cloud companies offer separate zones in the first place. Changing companies doesn't remove the risk. Using more than one zone does.

sim.title: Keep the ferry bookings up
sim.lede: You're Sol. The region has three availability zones. Choose where the two app servers go and whether the database gets a standby in another zone, then watch the morning's traffic: each dot is a request going through the load balancer, mostly ticket scans and timetable checks, with a new booking every 12 minutes, as on Tuesday night. Press Power loss in AZ-b and see what keeps serving. The clock starts at 04:00 and runs 120 times faster than real life, so a minute passes in half a second.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run it the way Sol built it, everything in AZ-b, and press Power loss when the clock reaches 04:12, as on Tuesday. Every request fails. Power returns 85 minutes later, at 05:37, and the app servers are up by 05:41, but the database's disk was damaged, so it has to be rebuilt from the 02:00 snapshot. The site stays down until 07:05, and the 11 bookings made after 02:00 are lost. Reset, put the app servers in AZ-a and AZ-c, keep the single database in AZ-b, and cut the power again: the servers are fine, but they have no database, and the bookings made since the snapshot are lost all the same. Then give the database a standby in AZ-c and try once more: about a minute and a half of errors while it fails over, then the site carries on, with no bookings lost.

explain.oneLine: The cloud didn't go dark. One data center in one zone lost power, and Greywater had put both app servers and its only database in that zone, so the power still running in the other two zones did it no good.

steps.title: The cloud is someone else's data centers.
steps.text: A data center is a building full of servers with its own power, cooling and network links. A cloud company owns many of them and rents out pieces by the hour, so you don't buy machines or wait for them to arrive. The machines are still real, in real buildings that can flood, overheat or lose power, just like the harbor office.

steps.title: Regions, zones and data centers.
steps.text: A region is one area of the world with several availability zones. Each zone is one or more data centers with their own power, cooling and network, kept miles from the other zones but linked to them by fast private fiber. The point is that a fire, a flood or a power cut in one zone shouldn't reach the others. Zones are the cloud's way of giving you separate buildings. Greywater used one.

steps.title: Virtual machines, and services someone else runs.
steps.text: A virtual machine is a whole computer made of software. The cloud company's real server runs a hypervisor that splits it into several VMs, each with its own operating system, and each VM lives in exactly one zone. Sol installed the database himself on a VM, so copies, backups and a standby were his job, and he had none. A managed service hands that job to the cloud company. A managed database can keep a standby in another zone, update it with every write as it happens, and fail over to it by itself.

steps.title: What happened on Tuesday.
steps.text: At 4:12 the data center in AZ-b holding Greywater's three VMs lost power. AZ-a and AZ-c were fine, and held nothing of Greywater's. Power came back at 5:37 and the app servers were up by 5:41, but the database VM's disk had been damaged, and the newest copy was the 2:00 AM snapshot. So the 11 bookings made after it were lost, and the site stayed down until 7:05. A standby in another zone would have taken over within a couple of minutes and lost nothing, because it receives every write as it happens.

steps.title: The same map on AWS.
steps.text: On AWS, a VM is an EC2 instance, and you pick its subnet, and with it its availability zone, when you launch it. A managed relational database is Amazon RDS, where a Multi-AZ deployment keeps a synchronous standby in a different zone and fails over automatically, typically in 60 to 120 seconds. Files go in Amazon S3, which by default stores each one across at least three zones. And an Application Load Balancer must be given subnets in at least two zones.

diagram.aria: The fix drawn on AWS's map. A load balancer with a node in every zone sends traffic to an EC2 instance in each of three Availability Zones, AZ-a, AZ-b and AZ-c, inside one AWS Region. An RDS primary database in AZ-a keeps a synchronous copy in an RDS standby in AZ-b, which takes over by itself. Amazon S3 stores files across three or more zones.

explain.caption: The fix on AWS's map. One app server per zone behind a load balancer that has a node in every zone, a managed database with a standby in a second zone, and files in S3, which keeps its own copies in at least three zones. Any one zone can go dark and the site keeps answering.

fix.title: The fix: use more than one zone, at every layer
fix.text: Run at least two app servers in at least two zones, behind a load balancer that spans those zones, and make sure each one can carry the traffic alone. Move the database to a managed service with a standby in another zone: it copies every write as it happens and fails over by itself, typically within a minute or two, with nothing lost. Keep the nightly snapshots too, stored outside the database's zone, because a standby copies mistakes as faithfully as it copies data. Then test it on a quiet night: fail the database over on purpose, stop one zone's app server, and watch the site keep answering.

limits: Several zones protect you from one zone failing, not the whole region. A region-wide problem, or a bug in your own code, takes every zone down together. Surviving that takes a second region, which costs far more and gets its own cases later.
A standby isn't a backup. It copies every write, including a bad one: a table deleted on the primary is deleted on the standby too. Keep snapshots, and test restoring them.

It costs more and isn't instant. You pay for servers in each zone and for a standby database that mostly waits, every write waits a little longer while it's copied, and a failover still means a minute or two of errors that the app must retry through.

head: Where it runs
Good
Bad
rows: Cheapest and simplest. The machines sit close together.
One power cut, flood or fire in that zone and everything goes at once, like Tuesday.
App servers in two or more zones, one database
Losing one zone's app server is a non-event.
The database still sits in one zone, so losing that zone still takes the site down.
Every layer in two or more zones, database with a standby
Any one zone can go dark: a minute or two of failover, no lost bookings.
Costs more: two of everything, and each write waits a little longer while the standby keeps up.

explain.seniorTake: The cloud doesn't make your servers reliable. It hands you separate buildings, and using them is your job. Ask of every part of the system: if this zone went dark right now, what would still answer? Wherever the answer is nothing, that's the next thing to fix.

realWorld.title: AWS us-east-1, December 22, 2021
realWorld.text: At 4:35 AM Pacific time on December 22, 2021, AWS reported EC2 launch failures and network connectivity problems for some instances in a single Availability Zone, USE1-AZ4, in its US-EAST-1 Region. At 5:01 AM it confirmed a loss of power within a single data center in that zone. Its summary that afternoon gave the times: power was lost at 4:11 AM PST and restored at 4:55 AM, which let most EC2 instances and EBS volumes recover. But the power loss had damaged some of the hardware, which engineers in the building had to fix, and AWS had recovered the vast majority of instances and volumes only by 2:30 PM. Some hardware could not be recovered at all, so AWS told customers still waiting to relaunch the instance or recreate the volume from a snapshot.

realWorld.title: Who else noticed
realWorld.text: The Register covered the outage the same day. It reported that Slack and Asana had problems as a result, and noted that AWS advises customers not to rely on a single Availability Zone, but that not every customer follows that advice, so when a zone fails, their servers and data become unavailable.

realWorld.title: What AWS's updates said about single-AZ services
realWorld.text: AWS's updates that morning, reproduced word for word by customers on their own status pages, said connectivity and power to other data centers in that zone, and to other zones in the Region, were not affected, and recommended failing away from USE1-AZ4 for anyone able to do so. At 5:39 AM AWS said that services hosting endpoints in the affected data center, such as single-AZ RDS databases and ElastiCache, would have seen impact during the event. At 6:51 AM single-AZ RDS databases were still seeing some impact, and at 9:28 AM AWS reported recovery for the majority of the affected ones.

realWorld.title: Why the zone was named USE1-AZ4
realWorld.text: AWS maps zone names like us-east-1a to physical zones at random for each account, so one account's us-east-1a may be a different place from another's. The AZ ID, like use1-az1, is the same in every account for the same physical zone. The status updates named the zone by its AZ ID, USE1-AZ4, which points to the same place for every customer.

realWorld.title: What RDS Multi-AZ does when a zone fails
realWorld.text: Amazon RDS documents that when a Multi-AZ DB instance has a planned or unplanned outage caused by an infrastructure defect, RDS automatically switches to a standby replica in another Availability Zone. Failover times are typically 60 to 120 seconds, though large transactions or a long recovery can make it longer. The failover changes the database's DNS record to point at the standby, so apps have to reconnect, and AWS warns that some Java setups cache DNS answers so long that they keep trying the old address: the same TTL problem from the first case of this season.

asked: What's the difference between a region and an availability zone?
How would you make a web app survive the loss of one data center?
interview.answer: A region is a geographic area. An availability zone is one or more data centers inside it with separate power, cooling and networking, far enough from the other zones to fail on its own, close enough to copy data between them synchronously. To survive losing one: run app servers in at least two zones behind a load balancer, with enough capacity in each to carry the load alone; run the database with a synchronous standby in another zone that fails over automatically, like RDS Multi-AZ, typically 60 to 120 seconds; keep files in a service that stores them across zones, like S3; and keep backups, because a standby copies mistakes too. Then say what it doesn't cover: a region-wide outage needs a second region, and every one of these steps costs money, so match it to what downtime actually costs the business.

terms.def: Renting computing, storage and databases from a cloud company over the internet, paying for what you use, instead of buying and running your own machines. Someone else's data centers.
A company that runs data centers and rents out servers, storage and services in them by the hour, such as AWS.
A building full of servers, with its own power, cooling and network links. Real buildings: they can flood, overheat or lose power.
One area of the world where a cloud company runs several availability zones. AWS calls them Regions.
One or more data centers inside a region, with their own power, cooling and network, miles from the other zones but linked to them by fast private fiber.
Short for availability zone. AZ-a, AZ-b and AZ-c in this story are the three zones of one region.
AWS's fixed name for a physical zone, like use1-az4, the same in every account. Zone names like us-east-1a can point to different zones in different accounts.
A whole computer made of software: one real server is split into several VMs, each with its own operating system. A VM lives in exactly one zone.
Short for virtual machine.
The software on a real server that splits it into virtual machines and keeps them apart.
A server running the application itself, here the booking app, which takes requests and reads and writes the database.
The ferry company's software for selling tickets and checking them at the dock.
The handheld device at the dock that reads a passenger's ticket and asks the booking system whether it's valid.
Services the cloud company runs for you, such as a managed database: it handles the servers, backups, software updates and failover, and you use the result.
A second copy of a database in another zone that receives every write as it happens and waits to take over if the first copy fails.
The copy of a database that the app reads and writes. A standby takes its place after a failover.
Switching to a standby automatically when the main copy fails. On RDS Multi-AZ it typically takes 60 to 120 seconds.
Copying each write to the standby before it counts as done, so the standby never falls behind. It makes each write a little slower.
Running something in two or more availability zones so it survives losing one. On Amazon RDS, a deployment with a standby in a different zone.
Running something in only one availability zone. Cheaper, but that zone failing takes it down.
A saved copy of a disk or database at one moment. Restoring it brings back that moment, and loses anything written after it.
A copy kept so you can restore data after it's lost or damaged, such as nightly snapshots. Unlike a standby, it lets you go back in time.
The cloud company's web page where you manage your machines and see their state.
Virtual private cloud: your own private network inside AWS, split into subnets, each in one availability zone. The VPC console lists them.
One part whose failure takes the whole system down, like one zone holding every server.
A slice of a cloud network's addresses that sits in one availability zone. Launching a server into a subnet puts it in that zone.
Simple Storage Service: AWS's service for storing files. Most of its storage classes keep each file across at least three availability zones.
What S3 calls a stored file, together with its name and details.
Elastic Block Store: a virtual disk AWS attaches to an EC2 instance. It lives in one availability zone.
A failure that reaches every zone in a region at once. Several zones don't protect against it. A second region can.
Running a system in two or more regions, with data copied between them, so it can survive losing a whole region. Much more costly and complex.
A popular programming language. Java programs keep their own cache of DNS answers, and some setups keep them far longer than the TTL says.
AWS's Region in Northern Virginia, in the United States.
Pacific Standard Time, the US West Coast's winter clock. AWS's status updates that day used it.
AWS's published write-up of a major outage: what happened, why, and what it is changing. Not every outage gets one.
A British technology news site.
A workplace chat app.
A project-tracking app for teams.
A cooperative: a business owned by its members, like the fishermen who run the auction next door.

atWork: Open the AWS console for your team's production account (read-only access is enough) and list the EC2 instances behind one important service, with each one's Availability Zone. If they all share a zone, that zone is a single point of failure. In the VPC console, each subnet also shows its AZ ID, like use1-az4, which is what you compare with other accounts or with AWS's status updates. Then open RDS and check that service's database: does Multi-AZ say Yes, and which secondary zone does it list? Finally, check that the load balancer has subnets in every zone the instances use. Write down what would still answer if any one zone went dark tonight.

recall.prompt: Greywater's two app servers and its database all sat in AZ-b, and AZ-b's data center lost power. Which change would have kept the booking site up?
options: App servers in two zones, and a database with a standby in another zone
recall.why: Only spreading every layer across zones survives losing one zone. Bigger machines in the same zone go dark together, and snapshots limit what's lost, not how long the site is down.

recall.prompt: Your company's checkout runs on two EC2 instances in one Availability Zone and a single-AZ RDS database. Your manager asks what happens if that zone loses power, and what you'd change. What do you say?

keyIdeas.idea: Everything is in one zone, so checkout goes down with it
Put instances in at least two zones behind a load balancer
Make the database Multi-AZ: a standby in another zone with automatic failover
It costs more, a failover still means a minute or two of errors, and you still need backups

recall.model: If that zone loses power, checkout stops completely: both instances and the only database are in it, so the other zones' power doesn't help us. I'd run the instances in at least two zones behind the load balancer, each able to carry the load alone, and switch the database to RDS Multi-AZ, so a synchronous standby in another zone takes over by itself, typically within 60 to 120 seconds, with no committed orders lost. The app should retry through that minute or two of errors. It costs more, a second database and more instances, and we keep our backups, because the standby copies mistakes too.

options: One or more data centers with their own power, cooling and network, kept apart from the other zones in the same region
A backup copy of your data
recall.why: A region holds several zones. Each zone is one or more data centers, separate enough that one zone's power cut or flood shouldn't reach the others, close enough to copy data between them quickly.

recall.prompt: Compared with installing a database yourself on a virtual machine, what does a managed database service such as Amazon RDS take off your hands?
options: Nothing: it's the same thing with a different name
Backups, software patching, failure detection and failover
recall.why: AWS says RDS manages backups, software patching, automatic failure detection and recovery, and offers a standby in another zone. Your queries and your table design are still yours.

recall.prompt: A teammate says: "We're on RDS Multi-AZ now, so we don't need backups anymore." What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: The standby copies every write, mistakes included: a deleted table is gone on both
Backups let you go back in time; a standby only has now
Multi-AZ covers a zone failing, not a region outage or bad data

recall.model: Multi-AZ protects you from losing a zone, not from losing data. The standby copies every write as it happens, so if someone deletes a table or a bug corrupts rows, the standby has the same damage a second later. Backups and snapshots are the only way back to how things were yesterday. And Multi-AZ doesn't cover a region-wide outage either. Keep the backups, keep a copy outside the database's zone, and test restoring one.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Sol rebuilt everything: three app servers, one per zone, behind the load balancer, and a managed database with a standby in another zone. It sailed through a power cut in AZ-a without anyone noticing. Then last week the cloud company had a problem across its whole North Coast region: for 50 minutes nothing in any of its three zones could be reached, and our booking site was down the whole time. Our owner wants to know why the new setup didn't save us, and whether we should copy everything to a second region.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why didn't the multi-zone setup help, and should Greywater add a second region?

keyIdeas.idea: Zones protect against one zone failing, not the whole region
Surviving a region outage needs a second region: copies of the data and a way to move traffic there
It costs much more and is complex, so weigh it against what 50 minutes of downtime costs
A cheaper middle step: backups in another region and a practiced recovery plan

coldCase.model: The new setup did its job: it protects against one zone going dark, which it survived in AZ-a. A problem across the whole region takes every zone down together, and nothing inside that region can help. Surviving that means a second region: a copy of the database kept up to date there (usually a little behind, because it's far away), app servers ready to run, and a way to send customers there, typically by changing DNS. That roughly doubles the cost and adds a lot of moving parts, so weigh it against what 50 minutes of no bookings really costs. A sensible middle step: copy backups to another region every night, write down and practice how to rebuild there, and keep the paper manifest routine sharp for the first sailing.
